comment: Our review engine on AACR-Bench, the corpus a direct competitor published.
**Why this corpus**: 200 real PRs, 10 languages, 1,505 expert-confirmed issues and **three context levels, the
third of which is Repo Level** - so **it measures cross-file behaviour, which is our distinctive claim**.
**And the caveat that belongs in the artifact**: **Alibaba built both the tool and the benchmark it wins on**,
and an independent party said so - *"an instrument that agrees with itself is not evidence."* **Their reported
absolute precision is 33.9%**, so **their 33.90-versus-7.23 gap and their 9x token claim are their measurements
on their corpus, not runs reproduced here.**
route: our engine reading each PR diff; no bot account installed
comparisonBasis: their published figures, not a run we performed

defectSubset.recallWithheld: the goldens carry no type label, so there is no defect-only golden subset to divide by; the headline recall is the only recall this corpus supports

scoring.protocol: one judge verdict per (finding, golden) pair, then a maximum bipartite matching per pull request; the same protocol for both reviewers in the same job

fileSemantic.note: the corpus arithmetic over this run’s pairwise verdicts; not an official score, because the judge still sees one pair rather than one file’s list
fileSemantic.operatingPoint: the same findings the headline figures are computed over

scoring.emissionRule: actionability gate: the range covers an added line AND (the suggestion names an action OR the finding quotes added code), AND the category profile floor

arms.file: one call per file per lane, at most 3 findings per file per lane
arms.pullRequest: one call per lane for the whole pull request, at most 12 findings for the pull request

scoring.registeredRule: the pull-request arm at 16 findings per pull request exceeds the competitor figure of 0.4500 F1 on the same corpus, same judge, same goldens; the file arm stays in the same job as the control
scoring.changedFrom: the previous protocol consumed each golden with the first finding that matched it, in judging order

idioms.why: 41 of 50 sampled missed goldens are remarks the five lanes never attempt, and each is decidable from the syntax of one construct

remarks.why: 386 of 724 goldens had one of our findings on their own path and were still judged not to address them; 29 of 50 read goldens are maintainability or convention remarks

coverage.protocol: per pull request, the golden indices the registered rule covered

rankedFindings.text: Forward-declared enum used as return type without definition :: `ArrowType` is forward-declared as `enum class ArrowType : int;` but `balloonArrow()` now returns it by value. A forward declaration of a scoped enum with a fixed underlying type is legal, but any translation unit that calls `balloonArrow()` and uses the returned value (e.g., comparing it, switching on it, or converting it) needs the complete enum definition. The header does not include the header that defines `ArrowType`, so callers that only include `Preferences.h` will fail to compile when they use the result, and the public API now exposes an incomplete type. This is a breaking change to the public interface: existing callers expecting `int` will no longer compile, and the enum's definition is not visible from this header.

Forward-declared enum class with fixed underlying type is fragile across translation units :: The header forward-declares `enum class ArrowType : int;` in namespace TechDraw. A scoped enum forward declaration with a fixed underlying type is legal, but it requires every translation unit that includes this header to see the same underlying type. If the definition in the core TechDraw module ever changes its underlying type (e.g. to `short` or `unsigned`), this forward declaration silently becomes an ODR violation and the return type of `prefDefaultArrow()` will mismatch the definition, producing undefined behavior at link time rather than a compile error. The Gui layer is now coupled to the exact representation of a core-layer enum.

Breaking change: unscoped enum ArrowType converted to scoped enum class :: ArrowType was an unscoped enum whose enumerators (FILLED_ARROW, OPEN_ARROW, TICK, DOT, OPEN_CIRCLE, FORK, FILLED_TRIANGLE, NONE) were visible in the TechDraw namespace and implicitly convertible to int. Changing it to `enum class` removes those namespace-level names and disables implicit int conversion, so every existing caller that writes `TechDraw::FILLED_ARROW`, assigns an ArrowType to an int, or relies on integer comparison will fail to compile. This is a breaking change to a public header exported via TechDrawExport and used across the TechDraw module.

Breaking change to public API: RefType enum converted to scoped enum :: Changing `enum RefType` to `enum class RefType` changes the type of `getRefType()` and `getRefTypeSubElements()` from `int` to `RefType`. This is a breaking change to the public API of `DrawViewDimension`: existing callers that compare the return value against `int` constants (e.g., `invalidRef`, `oneEdge`) or store it in an `int` will no longer compile, and any code that relied on implicit conversion to `int` (e.g., serialization, switch statements over ints) breaks. The enum values are also no longer accessible unqualified, so external code referencing `DrawViewDimension::oneEdge` must be updated to `DrawViewDimension::RefType::oneEdge`.

Public API break: getPrefArrowStyle return type changed from int to ArrowType :: QGIArrow::getPrefArrowStyle() changed its return type from int to ArrowType. Any caller outside this translation unit that stores the result in an int, compares it against an int constant, or forwards it to a function taking int will now either fail to compile or silently change behavior via implicit conversion. The header declaration must be updated in lockstep, and all call sites across the TechDraw Gui module must be audited; a return-type change on a public method is a source-incompatible API break.

Forward-declared enum used in public API without definition :: The header declares `enum class ArrowType : int;` as a forward declaration inside namespace TechDraw, but `prefBalloonArrow()` returns this type by value. Callers of `prefBalloonArrow()` in other translation units that only include this header cannot use the returned value (no enumerators visible, cannot switch on it, cannot convert it) without also including the header that defines `ArrowType`. This makes the public interface of the dialog depend on an out-of-band include and couples the GUI preference dialog's API to an incomplete type, which is fragile and will break any consumer that includes only this header.

For a conv layer the weight shape is (out_channels, in_channels, *kernel), so `self.lora_up.weight` will have shape (out_dim, rank, 1) rather than the (out_dim, rank) shape that `mat1` (from the checkpoint) has, and `copy_(mat1)` will fail with a size mismatch. rankedFindings.text: backdrop-filter blur on list items forces per-item GPU compositing :: Adding `backdropFilter: blur(8px)` to each history item in the list means every rendered row gets its own backdrop-filter layer. In a webview with many history items, this forces the compositor to blur the content behind each row on every scroll/paint, which is expensive and can cause jank on lower-end machines. The same blur is also applied to the empty-state box, which is static and cheap, but the per-item blur is the hot path.

Without this, a change that accidentally returns Empty.create() in the catch, or that throws a wrapped error, would pass unnoticed.

rankedFindings.text: Batched update writes undefined values for every unset field, clobbering existing state :: The previous code called updateGlobalState/storeSecret for every key unconditionally, but the new batched object includes every destructured field from apiConfiguration, including fields that are undefined when the caller only intends to update a subset. updateGlobalStateBatch iterates Object.entries(updates) and calls context.globalState.update(key, value) for each, so any key whose value is undefined is written as undefined, overwriting previously persisted values. The same applies to updateSecretsBatch: storeSecret(context, key, undefined) deletes the secret. rankedFindings.text: Batched secret updates pass undefined values to storeSecret, which deletes secrets instead of preserving them :: updateSecretsBatch maps every entry of the updates record to storeSecret(context, key, value). storeSecret's signature is `value?: string`, and VS Code's SecretStorage.update with undefined deletes the secret. In updateApiConfiguration, batchedSecretUpdates is built from destructured fields of apiConfiguration that may be undefined (e.g. when the caller only updates a subset of providers). Previously the same behavior existed per-key, but the batching now makes it a single all-or-nothing operation: any undefined field in the record wipes that secret, and because the whole record is always passed, every secret not present in the caller's apiConfiguration is deleted on every update. This silently destroys stored credentials for providers the caller did not intend to touch.

why: no quoted code from the added lines
rankedFindings.text: Encoding detection trusts chardet output without validation :: chardet.detect() returns a best-guess encoding that can be wrong or return a label iconv-lite does not support (e.g. 'ASCII', 'UTF-16LE' with BOM, or a null encoding for empty/short buffers). The detected value is passed straight to iconv.decode without checking iconv.encodingExists(), so a misdetected or unsupported label either throws at decode time or silently corrupts the file content (e.g. a UTF-8 file misdetected as windows-1252 will be decoded with mojibake). The same unvalidated encoding is later used to re-encode on save, so a wrong guess round-trips corruption into the user's file.

why: no quoted code from the added lines
rankedFindings.text: Binary files are decoded as text instead of rejected :: The default branch now reads the file into a buffer and calls chardet.detect on it before checking isBinaryFile. chardet almost always returns some encoding guess (e.g. 'UTF-8', 'windows-1252') for arbitrary binary data, so the `else` branch that calls isBinaryFile and throws `Cannot read text for file type` is effectively unreachable. Binary files (images, PDFs, archives) that previously threw now get passed to iconv.decode and returned as garbage text, which is then fed into the model context. The isBinaryFile check must run on the buffer before encoding detection, not only as a fallback when detection returns nothing.

rankedFindings.text: Non-UTF8 save path writes encoded buffer but skips the normal save path :: When fileEncoding is not utf8, the code writes the encoded buffer directly with fs.writeFile and then returns early from the save routine. This bypasses the normal document save (which applies the user's edits, formatting, and triggers diagnostics refresh), so the file on disk is written from normalizedPostSaveContent while the open editor buffer and the diagnostics computed above are not reconciled with the written bytes. Additionally, the cast `encodedBuffer as unknown as Uint8Array` hides that iconv.encode returns a Buffer, and the early return means the subsequent save/format logic never runs for non-UTF8 files.

rankedFindings.text: IPYNB extraction now decodes with a guessed encoding instead of utf8, breaking JSON.parse :: extractTextFromIPYNB previously read the notebook as utf8. It now runs chardet on the raw buffer and decodes with the detected encoding. Notebooks are JSON and must be UTF-8; a misdetection (e.g. windows-1252) produces a string that JSON.parse rejects, so valid .ipynb files fail to extract. The same unvalidated encoding label is also passed to iconv.decode here.

why: no quoted code from the added lines
rankedFindings.text: Auth state nonce is no longer consumed after validation, enabling replay :: validateAuthState previously cleared the stored nonce via resetAuthNonce() after a successful match, making each state value single-use. The new implementation only compares state to authService.authNonce and returns the result, so the nonce remains valid indefinitely. An attacker who observes or captures a valid state value (e.g. from a callback URL, logs, or referrer) can replay it in subsequent auth callback requests and have them accepted, defeating the CSRF protection the state parameter is meant to provide.

why: no quoted code from the added lines
rankedFindings.text: Auth nonce is now static for the lifetime of the service, breaking CSRF/state validation :: The nonce was previously regenerated on every createAuthRequest() call and reset to null after successful authentication. It is now a readonly field generated once at construction. Every auth request from this service instance therefore uses the same `state` value, so an attacker who learns or observes one nonce can replay it against any later auth request, defeating the state parameter's CSRF protection. The removed resetAuthNonce() also means the nonce is never invalidated after a successful login.

rankedFindings.text: Callback URL is no longer URL-encoded when set via searchParams :: The old code wrapped both `state` and `callback_url` in encodeURIComponent before interpolating them into the query string. The new code uses `authUrl.searchParams.set(...)`, which percent-encodes the value but does not double-encode an already-encoded value — however, the callback URL contains `://` and is now passed raw. More importantly, if `this._config.URI` already contains query parameters (e.g. a pre-existing `state` or `callback_url`), `searchParams.set` will silently overwrite them, and any existing query string is re-serialized by the URL parser, which can change the semantics of the configured URI. The auth server may receive a different callback_url than intended, breaking the auth flow.

rankedFindings.text: OAuth state parameter mismatch downgraded to user prompt, enabling CSRF/login-CSRF :: The state parameter is the CSRF protection for the OAuth callback. Previously a mismatch aborted the flow; now a mismatch only shows a warning and proceeds to store the token if the user clicks "Store". An attacker who can cause the victim's browser to hit the callback URI with an attacker-controlled code (login CSRF) gets the victim to bind the attacker's account token, and the warning text even displays the attacker-influenced `uri.path`. The check no longer enforces the security property it exists for.
